newsitem.title: JAPAN: OLYMPICS-TRAFFIC JAMS EMERGE AS MAJOR NAGANO HEADACHE.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-TRAFFIC JAMS EMERGE AS MAJOR NAGANO HEADACHE.

text.p: Traffic jams are emerging as one of the biggest headaches for organisers of the 1998 Winter Olympic Games.
"Japanese roads are very narrow and I'm very concerned about the problem," said Makoto Kobayashi, director general of the Nagano Olympic Organising Committee (NAOC).
"I think we might have traffic jams during the Games."

A key instruction by the International Olympic Committee to NAOC was to avoid traffic problems after a poor bus system created chaos for athletes, officials and the media at last year's Atlanta Olympics.
In a bid to avoid a repetition, a fleet of 1,300 buses with professional drivers has been organised.
But NAOC has less control over bottlenecks like Hakuba, where a pre-Olympic ski jumping competition last month was accompanied by a nightmare traffic jam.
Although the event, which attracted 21,000 spectators, finished by mid-afternoon, roads was still blocked in the evening as skiers and other visitors tried to leave the popular resort.
The 50-km (30-mile) drive to Nagano, normally a 50-minute commute, took some visitors more than two and a half hours.
Besides ski jumping, Hakuba will host Olympic cross-country skiing, Nordic combined and the men's and women's Alpine skiing downhill and super-G events.
Ski jumping is expected to attract capacity crowds of 45,000, the biggest sporting crowds of the Games, to cheer on a strong Japanese contingent.

Hakuba, a village of 9,000 set in the foothills of the northern Japan Alps, attracts 3.7 million visitors annually to its ski runs, hot springs and hiking trails, but is also renowned for its cluttered roads.

During the Olympics, spectators and skiers will be encouraged to use public transport to reach Hakuba and other venues, and traffic regulations including road closures, controlled lanes and one-way restrictions, will be enforced.
Special lanes will also be reserved for Olympic traffic.
But Kobayashi admitted skiers were unlikely to abandon their cars and hotel-keepers in Hakuba could not be asked to stop accepting guests.
"At the Lillehammer (Winter) Olympics, organisers said 'please don't use your cars' and people said 'all right, we won't'. We wish we could do that in Japan but people just wouldn't agree."

"Even if we create routes that keep traffic moving smoothly for Olympic people, there will be people criticising us because they can't use the roads," he said. "They'll say 'why are all these roads empty?'. We can't keep everybody happy."
Some skiers say transport worries could have been minimised by providing a satellite athletes village in Hakuba.

The Italian cross-country team, which swept all four races at a World Cup event in the resort last month, have already booked hotel rooms in Hakuba during the Olympics to spare skiers the commute from the athletes village in Nagano.
Walter Hofer, ski jumping co-ordinator for the International Ski Federation, said he expected all teams would lodge their competitors in Hakuba during the Olympics to avoid the traffic.
